references.text: Pharaoh asks Moses to pray to the Lord to remove the plague, following the same pattern as here with the hail plague.
Moses intercedes with the Lord on Pharaoh's behalf, parallel to the prayer to stop the hail.
Moses prays to the Lord, and the thunder and hail cease, fulfilling Pharaoh's request.
Pharaoh again asks Moses to pray to the Lord to remove the plague; the same expression 'pray to the Lord' is used.
Samuel is asked to pray to the Lord during a thunderstorm, a similar situation involving God's thunder.
Job is asked to intercede for others; the same Hebrew root for 'pray' (עתר) is used.
Simon asks the apostles to pray to the Lord on his behalf, a similar request for intercession.
Both verses directly link the Lord's thunder to judgment over sinful behavior as a sign of God's sovereignty.
Contrasting use of 'Now it is enough,' marking respectively human submission to God's power and God's final decision regarding a prophet's prayer.
Contrasting parallel: In Exodus, crying out to the Lord proves effective (the thunder stops), whereas in Judges the impotence of false gods is emphasized by crying out to them.
